title: MAHA’s Identity Crisis
author: David Moulton
content:
![MAHA’s Identity
Crisis](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/AP26092791333313.jpg)

In late October, Calley Means resigned from his position as senior advisor to
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. One of the
architects of the Make America Healthy Again movement, Means has continued to
praise both Kennedy and President Trump since his departure, but according to
[__Politico__](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/22/calley-means-top-maha-
ally-resigns-from-trump-administration-01132073?ref=compactmag.com) and _The
New York Times_ , he stepped down out of frustration that the White House was
siding with pesticide manufacturers, at odds with the movement's priorities.
It was just one sign that, two years into its alliance with Trump's GOP, MAHA
is going through an identity crisis. As _The Wall Street Journal_ recently
[_reported_](https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/the-maha-maga-alliance-is-
fracturing-before-the-midterms-27b9bcf7?ref=compactmag.com), MAHA-aligned
donors and PACS have largely steered clear of the midterm elections.

By some criteria, MAHA has been a success. In just a few years, it went from
being a minor dissident movement to having key allies in the White House and
Congress. However, many now seem to feel disillusioned by the compromises that
go along with being part of the establishment. A MAHA summit held in
Washington in September provoked a backlash from grassroots activists appalled
by the sponsorship of corporate giants like WalMart and UnitedHealth. None of
this should surprise us. MAHA was destined to disappoint because of the
political and philosophical contradictions at its core.
